report:
Conclusion: your view is not supported by the best current evidence. The claim is **probably true, but the benefit looks modest and context-dependent**. The key direct evidence is a large NEJM randomized trial at cesarean delivery finding chlorhexidine–alcohol produced a significantly lower surgical-site infection risk than iodine–alcohol: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048. A cesarean-focused systematic review/meta-analysis likewise concluded chlorhexidine–alcohol reduces SSI versus povidone-iodine solutions: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/. Cochrane is more cautious: moderate-certainty evidence that chlorhexidine before caesarean is “probably slightly” better than povidone iodine: https://www.cochrane.org/CD007462/PREG_skin-preparation-preventing-infection-following-caesarean-section.

Important caveat: not every trial agrees. A randomized trial of nonemergent cesarean birth found similar SSI rates for povidone–iodine, chlorhexidine with alcohol, and sequential use: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26551196/. Also, some reviews pool aqueous and alcohol-based povidone-iodine, so evidence is strongest for chlorhexidine–alcohol versus iodine–alcohol specifically from the NEJM trial, while broader comparisons suggest only a small average advantage. Overall: chlorhexidine–alcohol is a reasonable, evidence-supported choice, but not a guaranteed large effect in every setting.
